issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s continued legal control of a closed shop does not constitute occupation when the tenant stops the business and leaves the premises closed continuously without reasonable cause.
material_facts: The landlord alleged that the tenant had ceased using the shop for a continuous period of more than four months during the relevant years.
The tenant argued that the shop remained in his effective control, secured under his lock, and that temporary closure did not amount to cessation of occupation.
issues.conclusion: A tenant who stops the business carried on in a shop and closes it continuously for four months without reasonable cause is liable for eviction; legal possession or control alone does not amount to occupation for this purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(2)(v) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, cessation of occupation for a continuous period of four months without reasonable cause is an eviction ground. Read in context and in light of the purpose of preventing scarce buildings from remaining unused by tenants who do not need them, legal possession alone is not occupation.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_stopped_business and premises_closed_continuously_four_months and not reasonable_cause

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_stopped_business: The tenant stopped carrying on the business conducted in the premises.
predicates.premises_closed_continuously_four_months: The tenant left the premises closed continuously for at least four months.
predicates.reasonable_cause: There was a reasonable cause for the tenant to stop using and close the premises.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding concerns a tenant who stopped the business and kept the premises closed continuously for four months without reasonable cause, the tenant is liable for eviction.

issues.legal_issue: Non-occupation as an eviction ground must continue until the landlord files the eviction application.
material_facts: The tenant’s alleged non-occupation ended before the eviction application was filed.
The landlord filed the eviction application after the tenant had resumed occupation.
issues.conclusion: Because non-occupation did not continue until the filing of the eviction application, the eviction ground was not established, and the decisions ordering eviction were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(v) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, requires non-occupation to continue until the eviction application is filed. The Court relied on the present-perfect-tense reasoning in Goppulal v. Thakurji Shriji Shriji Dwarkadheeshji, distinguished Gajanan Dattatraya v. Sherbanu Hosang Patel, and noted that V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal removed the general requirement of a notice to quit before an eviction action. It followed Nathia Agarwalla v. Musst. Jahanara Begum in cautioning against using comparisons with rent statutes of other States as a guide to construction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on the basis of the tenant’s non-occupation.
predicates.nonoccupation_ended_before_eviction_appl: The tenant resumed occupation before the landlord filed the eviction application.

issues.definition: If a tenant resumes occupation before the landlord files a rent-control eviction application based on non-occupation, the eviction ground is not established.
